> \(d\) Vendor cooperates fully with the audit, including by providing access to relevant personnel, documentation, and systems, and by making reasonable workspace available to Pinnacle\'s audit team during on-site audits.

**Red line:** Audit rights limited to a single vendor facility (excluding subprocessor sites) are **unacceptable**. Such a limitation would prevent Pinnacle from verifying compliance at the locations where data processing actually occurs, particularly where the vendor relies on subprocessors for hosting, storage, or processing activities. If vendor refuses to extend audit scope to subprocessor facilities, the negotiator must escalate immediately to Margaret Yuen-Park.
**[8.2 HIPAA Audit Requirements]{.underline}**

Under HIPAA, Pinnacle as Covered Entity must be able to audit Business Associates for compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule and Privacy Rule. The DPA/BAA must expressly state that Pinnacle\'s audit rights include the right to evaluate vendor\'s HIPAA compliance, including without limitation:
> • Review of vendor\'s HIPAA risk assessments (required under 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A));
> • Review of vendor\'s workforce training records and training content;
> • Review of vendor\'s security incident logs and breach response records;
> • Review of vendor\'s policies and procedures related to PHI access, use, disclosure, and safeguarding;
> • Interviews with vendor\'s HIPAA Privacy Officer and HIPAA Security Officer (or equivalents); and
> • Inspection of physical and technical safeguards at facilities where ePHI is created, received, maintained, or transmitted.

The HIPAA audit right must be independent of and in addition to any general audit right under the DPA. If the DPA\'s general audit provision is narrower than what HIPAA requires, the BAA must include a separate, broader audit provision that addresses the HIPAA-specific requirements listed above.
**[Section 9: Data Return, Deletion, and Retention]{.underline}**

This Section addresses the provisions governing the disposition of data at the end of the vendor relationship, including the critical interplay between post-termination data deletion obligations and HIPAA\'s six-year record retention requirement. Getting these provisions right is essential to ensuring both a clean transition and ongoing regulatory compliance.
**[9.1 Data Return Option]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, for any reason, vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **data return option** --- that is, the right to receive a complete copy of all Personal Data, PHI, and California Personal Information processed by vendor under the DPA, in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, before any deletion occurs. The data return option must be exercisable at Pinnacle\'s sole election; vendor may not condition the return of data on payment of additional fees beyond those specified in the DPA/MSA, nor may vendor require Pinnacle to waive any rights or claims as a condition of data return.

**Must-have:** Vendor must provide **at least thirty (30) calendar days of transition assistance** following Pinnacle\'s request for data return, during which period vendor must: (i) continue to securely host and maintain Pinnacle\'s data in accordance with all security and confidentiality obligations of the DPA; (ii) cooperate in data migration activities, including by making data available for export through secure channels and in agreed-upon formats; (iii) make relevant vendor personnel available to support the transition, including technical staff familiar with the data structures and systems involved; and (iv) refrain from deleting any Pinnacle data until Pinnacle has confirmed in writing that the data return is complete.

**Must-have:** Following completion of data return (or upon Pinnacle\'s written instruction to proceed directly to deletion without return), vendor must **securely delete all copies** of Pinnacle data in vendor\'s possession, custody, or control, including copies in active systems, staging environments, archives, and backup media. Pinnacle\'s playbook target is deletion within **thirty (30) calendar days** following completion of data return or receipt of Pinnacle\'s deletion instruction; the maximum acceptable deletion window is **sixty (60) calendar days**. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **written certification of deletion** signed by an authorized officer of vendor, confirming that all copies of Pinnacle data have been securely deleted using methods consistent with NIST SP 800-88 or equivalent standards.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides data return in Pinnacle\'s preferred format (to be specified in the DPA or MSA), with all metadata intact and in a structure that facilitates import into Pinnacle\'s systems or a successor vendor\'s systems without material data loss or reformatting.

**Fallback:** If vendor insists on a longer deletion window (e.g., 90 days), this is acceptable only if: (i) the data return option is fully preserved; (ii) the 30-day transition assistance period is preserved; (iii) all security, confidentiality, and use restrictions of the DPA continue to apply to retained data throughout the extended deletion window; and (iv) vendor provides a written explanation of why 90 days is required (e.g., backup media rotation schedules).
**[9.2 HIPAA Record Retention]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must acknowledge and account for HIPAA\'s **six (6) year record retention requirement** under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later. The categories of documentation subject to this requirement include:
> • The BAA itself;
> • Policies and procedures related to the privacy and security of PHI;
> • Workforce training records and training materials;
> • Security incident and breach response records;
> • Risk assessments and risk management documentation;
> • Access logs and audit trails related to PHI; and
> • Any other documentation required to demonstrate compliance with HIPAA requirements.

**Must-have:** The six-year HIPAA retention obligation must be **expressly reconciled** with the post-termination deletion obligation set forth in Section 9.1 above. Without an express reconciliation, the deletion obligation and the retention obligation create an internal contradiction that could result in either premature deletion of HIPAA-required records or indefinite retention of PHI without adequate contractual protections. Pinnacle\'s recommended reconciliation language is as follows:

> *\"Notwithstanding the deletion obligations in this Section, Processor shall retain such records as are required to comply with HIPAA record retention requirements (45 CFR § 164.530(j)) for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when such records were last in effect, whichever is later. Such retained records shall remain subject to the confidentiality, security, and use restrictions of this Agreement and the Business Associate Agreement for the duration of the retention period. Upon expiration of the applicable retention period, Processor shall securely delete all such retained records and provide Controller with written certification of deletion.\"*

**Red line:** Any post-termination deletion clause that does not carve out HIPAA record retention requirements is **non-compliant** and creates significant regulatory risk. A vendor that deletes HIPAA-required documentation within 30 or 60 days of termination may be in violation of 45 CFR § 164.530(j), and Pinnacle could face enforcement consequences if it cannot produce required documentation during an OCR investigation. Negotiators must ensure that the HIPAA retention carve-out is included in every DPA involving PHI. If a vendor\'s DPA template contains a blanket deletion-at-termination clause without a HIPAA carve-out, the clause must be redlined before execution. Escalate immediately if the vendor refuses to include the carve-out.
**[Section 10: Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**

Governing law and dispute resolution provisions are critical in DPAs that cover both US and EU data, particularly where the vendor is a non-US entity. A DPA that applies a single non-US governing law and non-US dispute resolution forum to all disputes --- including disputes involving US PHI and California personal information --- could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to enforce its US regulatory rights and may be inconsistent with the jurisdictional framework of HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA enforcement. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required approach: a bifurcated governing law and dispute resolution structure.
**[10.1 Bifurcated Governing Law]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** DPAs covering both US and EU data must include a **bifurcated governing law clause** that applies different governing law depending on the nature of the claim and the data involved:

> **(a) US Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **US data** --- including PHI, ePHI, CCPA/CPRA-covered personal information, and any other personal data of US-based data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **State of Delaware**, without regard to its conflict of laws principles. Delaware law is Pinnacle\'s preferred governing law for US data disputes because Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation, Delaware has a well-developed body of commercial law, and the Delaware courts have extensive experience with complex commercial and data-related disputes.

> **(b) EU/EEA Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **EU/EEA data** --- including GDPR-covered personal data of EU/EEA data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **applicable EU/EEA Member State**. Where Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. is the contracting controller, the law of the **Netherlands** is preferred. Where the vendor is based in Germany and strongly resists Dutch law, **German law** is an acceptable alternative for EU data disputes.

**Nice-to-have:** Delaware law for all matters, including EU data disputes. However, this position is unlikely to be accepted by EU-based vendors and may conflict with GDPR mandatory provisions that require application of EU Member State law for certain data protection matters, including enforcement actions by supervisory authorities.

**Fallback:** German law for EU data disputes is acceptable, provided that Delaware law for US data disputes is preserved as a must-have. The bifurcation itself --- applying US law to US data disputes and EU law to EU data disputes --- is the critical structural requirement. Pinnacle will not accept a DPA that applies a single non-US governing law (e.g., German law) to disputes involving PHI or CCPA-covered personal information.
**[10.2 Dispute Resolution Forum]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** The DPA must include the following forum selection provisions:

> **(a) US Data Disputes.** The parties consent to the exclusive jurisdiction of the **United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, Austin Division**, or, where federal subject matter jurisdiction is unavailable, the **state courts of Travis County, Texas**, for all disputes arising from or related to the processing of US data. This forum selection reflects the location of Pinnacle\'s principal offices and the location of Pinnacle\'s primary US data processing operations.

> **(b) EU Data Disputes.** For disputes arising from or related to the processing of EU/EEA data, arbitration under recognized EU arbitration rules is acceptable. Pinnacle will accept arbitration administered by:
> • The **DIS** (Deutsche Institution für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit / German Institution of Arbitration) Rules, seated in Germany;
> • The **ICC** (International Chamber of Commerce) Arbitration Rules, seated in the relevant EU jurisdiction; or
> • The **LCIA** (London Court of International Arbitration) Rules, seated in the relevant EU jurisdiction.

**Nice-to-have:** Federal court jurisdiction (Western District of Texas) for all disputes, including EU data disputes. This is unlikely to be accepted by EU vendors but should be proposed as the opening position.

**Fallback:** Pinnacle will accept arbitration for EU data disputes but will **NOT** accept non-US arbitration or non-US courts for disputes involving US data (PHI, CCPA-covered data, or any other US personal information). Any vendor DPA that applies a non-US governing law and/or a non-US dispute resolution forum to US data disputes must be **redlined**. Escalate to Margaret Yuen-Park and Rachel Osterfeld (Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP) if the vendor insists on a non-US forum for US data disputes.

**Note for negotiators:** Some vendor templates apply a single governing law (e.g., German law) and a single arbitration forum (e.g., Munich) to all disputes under the DPA, regardless of the type of data or the jurisdiction of the affected data subjects. This approach is problematic for several reasons:

> • HIPAA enforcement is under **US federal jurisdiction**. An arbitration clause seated in Munich may not be enforceable against an OCR subpoena or investigation, and may create practical barriers to Pinnacle\'s enforcement of its HIPAA-related contractual rights.

> • CCPA/CPRA enforcement is under **California jurisdiction** (California Attorney General and the California Privacy Protection Agency). A German arbitration clause may create uncertainty regarding the enforceability of CCPA-related contractual provisions.
> • A blanket non-US forum clause could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to seek **injunctive relief** in US courts for urgent data protection matters, such as an ongoing unauthorized disclosure of PHI.

The bifurcated approach recommended in this Section addresses these concerns by ensuring that US data disputes are resolved in US forums under US law, while EU data disputes are resolved in EU forums under EU law.
**[Section 11: International Data Transfers]{.underline}**

While this playbook focuses primarily on US requirements, cross-border data transfers directly affect US data and must be addressed in vendor DPA negotiations. For example, EU data may be transferred to the US for disaster recovery or support purposes, and US data may be accessed remotely by vendor personnel located in the EU or other jurisdictions. The DPA must establish clear transfer mechanisms and documentation requirements for all such scenarios.
**[11.1 Transfer Mechanisms]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Where vendor or any subprocessor transfers personal data from the EU/EEA to a third country (including the United States), the DPA must specify the applicable lawful transfer mechanism for each transfer scenario. Acceptable transfer mechanisms include:

> **(a) EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021. The appropriate module must be selected for each transfer relationship:
> • **Module 2** (Controller-to-Processor): For transfers from Pinnacle EU B.V. (as Controller) to a vendor (as Processor) located outside the EEA;
> • **Module 3** (Processor-to-Subprocessor): For transfers from a vendor (as Processor) to a subprocessor located outside the EEA; and
> • **Module 4** (Processor-to-Controller): Where applicable, for reverse transfers.

> **(b) EU-US Data Privacy Framework (\"DPF\")** certification: Acceptable only if the receiving entity (vendor or subprocessor) is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities. Negotiators should verify the vendor\'s DPF certification status on the International Trade Administration\'s Data Privacy Framework List (dataprivacyframework.gov) before relying on this mechanism.
> **(c) Binding Corporate Rules (\"BCRs\")**: Acceptable where the vendor has approved BCRs in place that have been reviewed and approved by the competent EU supervisory authority.
**Must-have:** The DPA must address **all** transfer scenarios, including:
> • Primary data hosting and processing transfers (e.g., data stored in an EEA data center and processed by a US-based vendor);
> • Disaster recovery and business continuity transfers (e.g., data replicated to a US-based backup facility);
> • Remote access from third countries (e.g., vendor support engineers located in India, the Philippines, or the US accessing EU data from non-EEA locations); and
> • Subprocessor transfers (e.g., vendor engages a subprocessor in a third country to perform specific processing activities).

**Must-have:** Vendor must conduct and document a **Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\")** for each transfer of personal data to a third country. The TIA must assess the laws and practices of the recipient country that may affect the protection of the transferred data, including government surveillance laws, and must be made available to Pinnacle upon request. Where the TIA identifies risks that cannot be mitigated by supplementary measures, the transfer mechanism may need to be reconsidered.

**Must-have:** If a subprocessor is not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, SCCs must be executed with the appropriate module (typically Module 3, Processor-to-Subprocessor) before any personal data is transferred to that subprocessor.

**Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle pre-approves the specific SCC modules for each transfer relationship during DPA negotiation, ensuring clarity and reducing the need for post-execution amendments as transfer relationships evolve.

**Fallback:** If vendor\'s DPA template attaches only one SCC module (which is common), Pinnacle will require the addition of all applicable modules before execution. The negotiator should assess the vendor\'s transfer relationships and subprocessor arrangements to determine which modules are required and ensure that they are included in the DPA as executed.
**[Section 12: Subprocessing Requirements]{.underline}**

Vendors frequently engage subprocessors to perform specific data processing activities on their behalf. Because Pinnacle\'s data may ultimately be processed by entities with which Pinnacle has no direct contractual relationship, the DPA must include robust subprocessor requirements that ensure end-to-end protection. This Section works in conjunction with Section 8 (Audit Rights --- subprocessor coverage) and Section 4 (HIPAA BAA --- subcontractor flow-down).
**[12.1 Subprocessor Obligations]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Vendor must impose on each subprocessor **substantially the same** data protection obligations as those imposed on vendor under the DPA. This flow-down requirement applies to all applicable regulatory regimes, including:

> • **HIPAA BAA flow-down terms**: Each subprocessor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI must be bound by BAA obligations equivalent to those in vendor\'s BAA with Pinnacle (per 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));

> • **CCPA/CPRA Service Provider restrictions**: Each subprocessor that processes California personal information must be contractually restricted from selling, sharing, combining, or using the personal information for purposes other than those specified in the agreement;

> • **GDPR Article 28 requirements**: Each subprocessor must be bound by a written contract that provides the same level of data protection as the vendor\'s DPA with Pinnacle (per GDPR Art. 28(4)); and
> • **Confidentiality obligations**: Each subprocessor must be bound by confidentiality obligations at least as protective as those in the DPA.

**Must-have:** Vendor remains **fully liable** for the acts and omissions of its subprocessors. The DPA must include an express statement that vendor shall be responsible for the performance of its subprocessors as if such acts or omissions were vendor\'s own. The use of subprocessors does not relieve vendor of any of its obligations under the DPA.
**Must-have:** The DPA must include a **current list of all authorized subprocessors**, specifying for each subprocessor:
> • Name and corporate entity;
> • Location (country and, where relevant, specific data center location);
> • Services provided to vendor in connection with Pinnacle\'s data; and
> • Description of the data processing activities performed by the subprocessor.
This list must be appended to the DPA as an exhibit or schedule and must be updated whenever a subprocessor is added, removed, or changed.

**Must-have:** Pinnacle (as Controller) must be notified of any proposed new subprocessor or change to existing subprocessors with **sufficient time to assess and object** to the change before it becomes effective. The DPA must provide Pinnacle with a meaningful objection right --- that is, the right to object to a proposed subprocessor and, if the objection is not resolved, the right to terminate the DPA without penalty.

**Nice-to-have:** A **thirty (30) day objection window** for new subprocessors, measured from the date of vendor\'s notification to Pinnacle. This provides Pinnacle with adequate time to assess the proposed subprocessor\'s data protection capabilities, conduct due diligence, and raise any concerns before the subprocessor begins processing Pinnacle\'s data.

**Fallback:** An objection window of **fourteen (14) to fifteen (15) calendar days** is acceptable and is consistent with current market norms for DPA negotiations. However, the objection window must not be shorter than fourteen (14) days, and the notification must include sufficient detail about the proposed subprocessor (including the information listed above) to enable Pinnacle to make an informed assessment.
**[Section 13: Security Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section sets forth the minimum security standards that must appear in every Pinnacle vendor DPA. These requirements apply to all vendors that process Pinnacle\'s data, regardless of the regulatory regime applicable to the data.
**[13.1 Technical and Organizational Measures]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** The DPA must reference and incorporate the following security frameworks:

> **(a) GDPR Article 32** --- Vendor must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons. This reference is required for all DPAs involving EU/EEA data and is good practice for all DPAs.
> **(b) HIPAA Security Rule categories** --- Where vendor is a Business Associate, the DPA/BAA must require implementation of:

> • **Administrative safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.308, including security management processes, assigned security responsibility, workforce security, information access management, security awareness and training, security incident procedures, contingency planning, evaluation, and business associate contracts;
> • **Physical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.310, including facility access controls, workstation use, workstation security, and device and media controls; and
> • **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity mechanisms, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.

> Both the GDPR and HIPAA security frameworks must be explicitly referenced in the DPA. A DPA that references only GDPR Article 32 without addressing the HIPAA Security Rule is insufficient for vendors that process PHI.
**Must-have:** The DPA must require the following specific security measures:
> • **Encryption at rest**: Minimum AES-256 encryption for all Pinnacle data at rest, including data stored on servers, databases, storage arrays, and backup media;
> • **Encryption in transit**: Minimum TLS 1.2 for all data in transit, with **TLS 1.3 preferred**. Use of deprecated protocols (SSL, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) is prohibited;

> • **Access controls**: Role-based access controls (\"RBAC\") based on the principle of least privilege, ensuring that only authorized personnel with a legitimate business need may access Pinnacle\'s data. Access must be reviewed and recertified at least quarterly;
> • **Multi-factor authentication**: Required for all remote access to systems containing Pinnacle data and for all administrative or privileged access.

**Must-have:** Vendor must hold a current **ISO 27001 certification** or equivalent information security management system certification, and must provide **SOC 2 Type II reports** covering the relevant service at least annually. Reports and certifications must be provided to Pinnacle within thirty (30) days of request.

**Nice-to-have:** Annual **penetration testing** conducted by a qualified third-party firm, with a summary of findings and remediation activities provided to Pinnacle. This is market standard and should be readily achievable by any vendor with a mature security program. Vendor should also agree to implement additional security measures as reasonably requested by Pinnacle to address evolving threats, emerging vulnerabilities, or changes in applicable law or regulatory guidance.
**[Section 14: Data Subject / Consumer Rights Assistance]{.underline}**

Pinnacle has obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR to respond to requests from individuals (patients, consumers, and data subjects) exercising their data protection rights. Because vendors often hold or process the data necessary to respond to these requests, vendor cooperation is essential. This Section sets forth the requirements for vendor assistance with data subject and consumer rights requests.
**Must-have:** Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding to data subject and consumer rights requests under all applicable regulatory regimes, including but not limited to:

> **HIPAA --- Individual Access Rights.** Under 45 CFR § 164.524, individuals have the right to access their PHI. Pinnacle must provide access within **thirty (30) days** of the request, with one **thirty (30) day extension** permitted upon written notice to the individual. Vendor must cooperate with Pinnacle to identify, locate, and produce the requested PHI within a timeframe that enables Pinnacle to meet this regulatory deadline.

> **CCPA/CPRA --- Consumer Rights.** Under the CCPA/CPRA, California consumers have the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), and the right to limit use of sensitive personal information (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.121). Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in fulfilling these requests, including by searching vendor\'s systems for the consumer\'s personal information, executing deletion or correction instructions, and confirming completion.

> **GDPR --- Data Subject Rights.** Under the GDPR, data subjects have the right of access (Art. 15), the right to rectification (Art. 16), the right to erasure (Art. 17), the right to restriction of processing (Art. 18), the right to data portability (Art. 20), and the right to object (Art. 21). Pinnacle/Pinnacle EU B.V. must respond to data subject requests within **thirty (30) days** per GDPR Art. 12(3), with a possible extension of two additional months for complex or numerous requests. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding within this timeframe.

**Must-have:** Vendor\'s assistance timeline must be **short enough** to allow Pinnacle to meet its own regulatory deadlines. Given the regulatory timelines above, vendor delay in responding to Pinnacle\'s requests for assistance could result in Pinnacle missing a statutory deadline, with potential enforcement consequences.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor responds to Pinnacle\'s data subject/consumer rights assistance requests within **five (5) business days** of receipt. This provides Pinnacle with a meaningful buffer before its own regulatory deadlines expire.

**Fallback:** A response timeline of **ten (10) business days** is acceptable, provided that vendor commits to best efforts to respond sooner where Pinnacle indicates that the request is time-sensitive.
**[Section 15: DPA Term, Survival, and Termination Provisions]{.underline}**
This Section addresses the DPA\'s term, its relationship to the underlying MSA, and the critical question of which provisions survive termination and for how long.

**Must-have:** The DPA should be **coterminous with the MSA**. The DPA should become effective upon execution of the MSA (or, if later, upon the date the vendor first processes Pinnacle data) and should remain in effect until the MSA terminates or expires, unless terminated earlier in accordance with its terms. If the MSA is renewed or extended, the DPA should automatically renew or extend for the same period.
**Must-have:** The following DPA provisions must **survive termination** of the DPA and the MSA for a period sufficient to cover all applicable regulatory obligations:
> • **Breach notification** obligations (Section 5);
> • **Data return and deletion** obligations (Section 9);
> • **Liability and indemnification** obligations (Section 6);
> • **Audit rights** (Section 8), to the extent necessary to verify compliance with post-termination obligations;
> • **Confidentiality** obligations, for as long as vendor retains any Pinnacle data; and
> • **HIPAA BAA obligations**, for as long as vendor retains any PHI, and in any event for the six (6) year record retention period under 45 CFR § 164.530(j).

**Note on HIPAA Survival:** HIPAA requires six (6) years of record retention under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Any DPA survival period shorter than six (6) years may be insufficient for HIPAA purposes, because the termination of the DPA\'s protective provisions before the end of the retention period would leave PHI-related documentation without contractual protections. Where a vendor proposes a shorter survival period (e.g., two (2) years), Pinnacle must negotiate either:
> \(a\) An extension of the general DPA survival period to six (6) years; or

> \(b\) A carve-out providing that HIPAA-related obligations (including the BAA, security obligations, audit rights, and confidentiality obligations as they relate to PHI) survive for the full **six (6) year retention period** or for as long as vendor retains any PHI, whichever is longer, even if the general DPA survival period is shorter.

**Fallback:** A general DPA survival period of **two (2) to three (3) years** is acceptable for non-HIPAA obligations, provided that HIPAA obligations have a separate, longer survival as described above. The negotiator should ensure that the survival clause clearly distinguishes between the general survival period and the HIPAA-specific survival period, and that the HIPAA survival is not inadvertently overridden by the general survival provision.

**Category**            **Criteria**                                                                                                              **Approver**

**Complex DPAs**        Annual fees \$1,000,000--\$5,000,000; or involves PHI; or involves cross-border transfers                                 Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel

**[16.2 Red-Line Triggers Requiring Escalation]{.underline}**
The following situations constitute red-line triggers that require **immediate escalation** to Margaret Yuen-Park, regardless of the DPA\'s tier classification:
> \(a\) **Vendor refuses to execute a BAA** where vendor processes PHI;
> \(b\) **Vendor proposes a liability cap below 2x annual fees** for data protection claims;

> \(d\) **Vendor applies non-US governing law** to US data disputes (i.e., disputes involving PHI or CCPA-covered personal information);

In each of these situations, the negotiator must document the vendor\'s position in writing, provide a brief risk assessment, and forward the matter to the General Counsel\'s office for determination. **[Appendix B: Approved Template Language]{.underline}**

The following sample clause language is provided for use by Pinnacle negotiators when redlining vendor DPA templates. These are starting-point templates; all DPA language must be reviewed in the context of the specific vendor agreement and may require modification based on the specific facts and circumstances of the engagement.
**[B.1 BAA Integration Clause]{.underline}**

*\"This Data Processing Agreement incorporates the Business Associate Agreement attached hereto as Exhibit \[\_\] (the \'BAA\'), which is hereby made an integral part of this Agreement. In the event of any conflict between the terms of this Agreement and the terms of the BAA with respect to the processing, use, or disclosure of Protected Health Information (as defined in 45 CFR § 160.103), the more protective provision shall govern. The BAA shall remain in effect for the duration of this Agreement and, to the extent Processor retains any Protected Health Information following termination, for so long as Processor maintains such Protected Health Information.\"*
**[B.2 24-Hour Breach Notification Clause]{.underline}**

*\"Processor shall notify Controller of any actual or reasonably suspected Security Incident, Personal Data Breach, or Breach of Unsecured Protected Health Information (each, an \'Incident\') without undue delay and in any event within twenty-four (24) hours of Processor\'s discovery of such Incident. For purposes of this provision, an Incident shall be treated as discovered on the first day on which the Incident is known to Processor or, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to Processor. Notification shall be directed to Controller\'s Chief Privacy Officer at privacy-incidents@pinnaclehealth.com and by telephone at (512) 555-0199.\"*
**[B.3 Liability Cap Clause (2x Annual Fees with Willful Misconduct Carve-Out)]{.underline}**

*\"Processor\'s aggregate liability for all claims arising under or in connection with this Data Processing Agreement shall not exceed an amount equal to two times (2x) the total fees paid or payable by Controller to Processor during the twelve (12) month period immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the liability cap set forth in this Section shall not apply to claims arising from: (a) Processor\'s willful misconduct or gross negligence; (b) Processor\'s intentional or reckless breach of confidentiality obligations; or (c) regulatory fines, penalties, or enforcement costs imposed on Controller as a direct result of Processor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws.\"*
**[B.4 CCPA/CPRA Service Provider Certification Clause]{.underline}**

*\"Processor certifies that it understands and will comply with the following restrictions: (a) Processor shall not sell or share (as those terms are defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140) any Personal Information received from Controller; (b) Processor shall not retain, use, or disclose Personal Information for any purpose other than performing the services specified in this Agreement; (c) Processor shall not retain, use, or disclose Personal Information outside of the direct business relationship between Controller and Processor; and (d) Processor shall not combine Personal Information received from Controller with Personal Information received from any other source, except as expressly permitted under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag).\"*
**[B.5 Audit Rights Clause (Including Subprocessor Coverage)]{.underline}**

*\"Controller shall have the right, at its own expense and upon reasonable prior written notice (not less than fifteen (15) days for planned audits, and without notice for for-cause audits following a confirmed or suspected Incident), to audit Processor\'s and each Subprocessor\'s compliance with this Agreement, including by inspecting data processing facilities, reviewing policies and procedures, and examining relevant records. Processor shall contractually require each Subprocessor to submit to audits by Controller or Controller\'s designated auditor on terms no less favorable than those set forth in this Section.\"*
**[B.6 Data Return and Transition Assistance Clause]{.underline}**

*\"Upon termination or expiration of this Agreement, Processor shall, at Controller\'s election: (a) return to Controller a complete copy of all Personal Data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format; or (b) securely delete all copies of Personal Data. Where Controller elects data return, Processor shall provide at least thirty (30) calendar days of transition assistance following Controller\'s request, during which Processor shall continue to securely host the data and cooperate in data migration. Following completion of data return (or upon Controller\'s written instruction to proceed directly to deletion), Processor shall delete all remaining copies within thirty (30) days and provide written certification of deletion.\"*
**[B.7 Bifurcated Governing Law Clause]{.underline}**

*\"This Agreement shall be governed by: (a) with respect to all disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of US Data (including Protected Health Information and Personal Information of California residents), the laws of the State of Delaware, without regard to conflict of laws principles; and (b) with respect to all disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of EU/EEA Data, the laws of the Netherlands. For purposes of this provision, \'US Data\' means any Personal Data of data subjects located in the United States, and \'EU/EEA Data\' means any Personal Data of data subjects located in the European Economic Area.\"*

499: **[ANNEX B --- TECHNICAL AND ORGANIZATIONAL MEASURES]{.underline}**
500: 
501: This Annex B forms an integral part of the Data Processing Agreement (\"DPA\") and describes the technical and organizational measures implemented by the Processor to ensure the security and protection of Personal Data Processed on behalf of the Controller. These measures are designed to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, in accordance with Article 32 of the GDPR, and are subject to ongoing review and improvement.
502: 
503: **B.1 Encryption. Encryption at Rest:** All Personal Data stored in the Processor\'s data centers, including data stored in databases, file systems, object storage, and backup media, is encrypted at rest using the Advanced Encryption Standard with 256-bit keys (AES-256). Encryption at rest is applied uniformly across all storage tiers and replication targets, including primary storage in Frankfurt, secondary storage in Dublin, and disaster recovery storage in Northern Virginia.
504: 
505: **Encryption in Transit:** All data transmissions involving Personal Data are encrypted in transit using Transport Layer Security version 1.3 (TLS 1.3) or higher. This includes transmissions between the Controller\'s systems and the Processor\'s cloud infrastructure, transmissions between the Processor\'s data centers (Frankfurt, Dublin, and Northern Virginia), and transmissions between the Processor and its Subprocessors. The Processor does not support deprecated encryption protocols (including SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1) for any connections involving Personal Data.
506: 
507: **Key Management:** Encryption keys are managed through a centralized key management system utilizing FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security modules (HSMs). Encryption keys are generated using cryptographically secure random number generators, stored in the HSMs, and rotated on an annual basis in accordance with the Processor\'s key rotation policy. Key access is restricted to authorized personnel on a strict need-to-know basis, with all key management operations logged and auditable.
508: 
509: **B.2 Access Controls**
510: 
511: **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC):** The Processor implements role-based access control with least-privilege principles for all systems that Process Personal Data. Access to Personal Data is granted only to those personnel whose roles require such access for the performance of the Services, and access privileges are limited to the minimum level necessary for the performance of the assigned role.
512: 
513: **Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):** Multi-factor authentication is required for all administrative and privileged access to systems that Process Personal Data. MFA is enforced through hardware tokens or authenticator applications; SMS-based authentication is not permitted for privileged access.
514: 
515: **Segregation of Duties:** Critical Processing activities, including database administration, key management, and access provisioning, are subject to segregation of duties controls. No single individual has the ability to perform all steps of a critical operation without independent verification or approval.
516: 
517: **Access Reviews:** The Processor\'s information security team conducts formal access reviews on a quarterly basis to verify that access privileges remain appropriate and aligned with current role assignments. Access that is no longer required is promptly revoked. Access review results are documented and retained for a minimum of three (3) years.
518: 
519: **B.3 Network Security**
520: 
521: **Firewalls and Network Segmentation:** The Processor\'s data centers employ multi-layered firewall architectures with network segmentation between client environments, management networks, and public-facing services. Each client environment is logically isolated from other client environments and from the Processor\'s internal management infrastructure.
522: 
523: **Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS):** The Processor deploys intrusion detection and prevention systems across all network segments. IDS/IPS systems are monitored continuously (24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year) by the Processor\'s security operations center (SOC). Alerts are triaged and escalated in accordance with the Processor\'s incident response procedures.
524: 
525: **Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing:** Automated vulnerability scanning is performed on a monthly basis across all systems and network segments that Process Personal Data. Critical and high-severity vulnerabilities are remediated within fourteen (14) calendar days of identification; medium-severity vulnerabilities are remediated within thirty (30) calendar days. Annual penetration testing is conducted by an independent, qualified third-party information security firm. Penetration test findings are reported to the Processor\'s Chief Information Security Officer and tracked to remediation.
526: 
527: **DDoS Mitigation:** The Processor employs distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) mitigation services to protect its cloud infrastructure and the Controller\'s hosted applications from volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DDoS attacks.
528: 
529: **B.4 Physical Security**
530: 
531: **Data Center Security:** All data centers utilized by the Processor (including subprocessor-operated data centers in Dublin and Northern Virginia) are equipped with the following physical security controls:
532: 
533: > • 24/7 on-site security personnel
534: >
535: > • Closed-circuit television (CCTV) surveillance with a minimum of ninety (90) days of recorded footage retention
536: >
537: > • Biometric access controls (fingerprint or iris scan) at all entry points to data processing areas
538: >
539: > • Mantrap (airlock) entry systems at primary data center entrances
540: >
541: > • Visitor management procedures requiring escort by authorized personnel at all times
542: 
543: **Environmental Controls:** Data centers are equipped with:
544: 
545: > • Fire detection and suppression systems (pre-action dry pipe sprinkler systems and gas-based suppression for server rooms)
546: >
547: > • Climate control systems maintaining optimal temperature and humidity for computing equipment
548: >
549: > • Redundant power supply, including uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems and on-site diesel generators with a minimum of seventy-two (72) hours of fuel reserve
550: >
551: > • Redundant network connectivity from multiple independent telecommunications providers
552: 
553: **B.5 Data Center Locations**
554: 
555: The Processor\'s data processing infrastructure is distributed across the following data center locations:
556: 
557:   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
558:   **Data Center**          **Location**                                  **Operator**                                 **Role**
559:   ------------------------ --------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
560:   Frankfurt, Germany       Frankfurt am Main, Hesse, Germany             Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH             Primary EU data center --- production environment, primary data storage
561: 
562:   Dublin, Ireland          Dublin 2, Ireland                             Orionis Analytics Ltd. (Subprocessor)        Secondary EU data center --- anonymization and analytics processing
563: 
564:   Northern Virginia, USA   Fairfax, Virginia, United States of America   Larkfield Data Systems, LLC (Subprocessor)   Disaster recovery data center --- database management, backup, and failover
565:   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
566: 
567: **B.6 Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery**
568: 
569: **Geographic Redundancy:** Personal Data is replicated across geographically redundant data centers (Frankfurt, Dublin, and Northern Virginia) to ensure availability and resilience in the event of a localized outage, natural disaster, or other disruption affecting a single data center.
570: 
571: **Recovery Point Objective (RPO):** The Processor maintains a recovery point objective of one (1) hour, meaning that in the event of a disaster or system failure, the maximum data loss shall not exceed one (1) hour of data.
572: 
573: **Recovery Time Objective (RTO):** The Processor maintains a recovery time objective of four (4) hours, meaning that in the event of a disaster or system failure affecting the primary production environment, the Processor targets restoration of Services within four (4) hours.
574: 
575: **Disaster Recovery Testing:** The Processor conducts comprehensive disaster recovery testing at least once per year, including simulated failover to the Northern Virginia disaster recovery site. Test results are documented and reviewed by the Processor\'s Chief Information Security Officer and Chief Technology Officer.
576: 
577: **B.7 Personnel Security**
578: 
579: **Background Checks:** All Processor personnel who have access to Personal Data are subject to background checks prior to commencing employment or engagement, including verification of identity, criminal records checks (to the extent permitted by applicable law), and verification of professional qualifications where relevant.
580: 
581: **Confidentiality Agreements:** All Processor personnel with access to Personal Data are required to execute written confidentiality agreements in accordance with Section 4 of the DPA.
582: 
583: **Security Awareness Training:** All Processor personnel receive annual security awareness training covering topics including data protection principles, information security policies and procedures, social engineering and phishing awareness, incident reporting procedures, and secure data handling practices. Training completion records are maintained by the Processor\'s human resources department.
584: 
585: **B.8 Incident Response**
586: 
587: **Incident Response Plan:** The Processor maintains a documented incident response plan that is reviewed and updated at least annually. The incident response plan addresses the identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review of security incidents, including Personal Data Breaches.
588: 
589: **Incident Response Team:** The Processor maintains a designated incident response team that is available twenty-four (24) hours a day, seven (7) days a week, three hundred sixty-five (365) days a year. The incident response team includes representatives from information security, legal, operations, and communications functions.
590: 
591: **Alignment with ISO 27001:** The Processor\'s incident response procedures are aligned with the requirements of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, specifically Annex A Control A.5.24 (Information security incident management planning and preparation), A.5.25 (Assessment and decision on information security events), A.5.26 (Response to information security incidents), and A.5.27 (Learning from information security incidents).
592: 
593: **B.9 Certifications and Audits**
594: 
595: **ISO 27001:2022 Certification:** The Processor holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification, Certificate Number ISO-27001-SC-2024-0891, issued by TÜV Rheinland AG on June 15, 2024, valid through June 14, 2027. The certification covers the Processor\'s information security management system as it applies to the provision of cloud hosting, managed database, and analytics services from the Processor\'s Frankfurt data center.
596: 
597: **SOC 2 Type II Report:** The Processor obtains an annual SOC 2 Type II report covering the Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy). The most recent SOC 2 Type II report was dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, and was issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH. The SOC 2 Type II report is available to the Controller upon request, subject to the execution of a non-disclosure agreement where required by the Processor\'s auditor.
598: 
599: **Ongoing Compliance:** The Processor is committed to maintaining its ISO 27001 certification and obtaining annual SOC 2 Type II reports throughout the term of the DPA. The Processor shall promptly notify the Controller of any material findings, qualifications, or exceptions identified in any certification audit or SOC 2 examination that are relevant to the Processing of Personal Data on behalf of the Controller.
600: 
601: *End of Annex B --- Technical and Organizational Measures*

If such modification is not possible, the invalid provision shall be severed and the remaining provisions shall be interpreted so as to give effect to the Parties\' original intent to the maximum extent possible.

**17.4 Waiver.** No failure or delay by either Party in exercising any right, power, or privilege under this DPA shall operate as a waiver thereof, nor shall any single or partial exercise of any right, power, or privilege preclude any other or further exercise thereof or the exercise of any other right, power, or privilege.

**17.5 Notices.** All notices, requests, demands, and other communications required or permitted under this DPA shall be in writing and shall be delivered by hand, by internationally recognized overnight courier service, or by email to the addresses specified in this DPA or such other addresses as a Party may designate in writing from time to time. Notices shall be deemed received upon actual receipt.

**17.6 Assignment.** Neither Party may assign or transfer this DPA, or any of its rights or obligations hereunder, without the prior written consent of the other Party, except that either Party may assign this DPA to an affiliate or in connection with a merger, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all of its assets, provided that the assignee agrees in writing to be bound by the terms of this DPA.

**17.7 Counterparts.** This DPA may be executed in any number of counterparts, each of which shall be deemed an original, and all of which together shall constitute one and the same instrument. Execution and delivery of this DPA by electronic signature or by exchange of PDF copies shall have the same force and effect as execution and delivery of an original signed counterpart.
**[SIGNATURE BLOCK]{.underline}**
**IN WITNESS WHEREOF**, the Parties have caused this Data Processing Agreement to be executed by their duly authorized representatives as of the dates set forth below.
**CONTROLLER:**
\[Full Legal Name of Controller\]
**PROCESSOR:**
STRATOSPHERE CLOUD SERVICES GmbH Hohenzollernstraße 88, 80796 Munich, Germany Handelsregister HRB 247891, Amtsgericht München
**[ANNEX A --- DESCRIPTION OF PROCESSING]{.underline}**

This Annex A forms an integral part of the Data Processing Agreement (\"DPA\") and describes the Processing of Personal Data carried out by the Processor on behalf of the Controller in connection with the Services provided under the Agreement.
**A.1 Controller(s).**
**Field**                                     **Details**
**Name**                                      \[To be completed by the Controller\]
**Address**                                   \[To be completed by the Controller\]
**Contact Person**                            \[To be completed by the Controller --- name, position, email, telephone\]
**Activities Relevant to Data Transferred**   \[To be completed by the Controller --- description of the Controller\'s activities in connection with the Services\]
**Role**                                      Controller (within the meaning of Article 4(7) GDPR)
**Signature and Date**                        **\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_**
**A.2 Processor(s).**
**Field**                                     **Details**
**Name**                                      Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH
**Address**                                   Hohenzollernstraße 88, 80796 Munich, Germany
**Contact Person**                            Dr. Annika Vogt, Data Protection Officer (dpo@stratospherecloud.example.com; Tel: +49 89 2155 4450)
**Activities Relevant to Data Transferred**   Cloud hosting services, managed database services, and analytics support provided pursuant to the Agreement
**Role**                                      Processor (within the meaning of Article 4(8) GDPR)
**A.3 Subject Matter of Processing**

The subject matter of the Processing is the provision of cloud infrastructure services, managed database services, and analytics support services by the Processor to the Controller pursuant to the Agreement. The Processor hosts the Controller\'s applications and databases on the Processor\'s cloud infrastructure and provides managed database administration, optimization, backup, disaster recovery, and anonymized analytics reporting in connection with the Controller\'s healthcare platform operations.
**A.4 Duration of Processing**

The Processing shall be carried out for the duration of the Agreement, including any renewals or extensions thereof, and shall continue until the deletion or return of all Personal Data by the Processor in accordance with Section 12 of the DPA.
**A.5 Nature of Processing**
The Processing includes the following operations performed on Personal Data in connection with the Services:
> • Collection and ingestion of Personal Data from the Controller\'s systems into the Processor\'s cloud infrastructure
> • Storage and hosting of Personal Data in the Processor\'s data centers
> • Recording, organization, and structuring of Personal Data within managed databases
> • Retrieval and consultation of Personal Data in response to authorized queries from the Controller\'s applications
> • Use of Personal Data for the purpose of providing managed database services, including optimization, indexing, and performance tuning
> • Disclosure by transmission of Personal Data between the Processor\'s data centers (Frankfurt, Dublin, and Northern Virginia) for purposes of redundancy, disaster recovery, and load balancing
> • Alignment and combination of Personal Data as necessary for analytics processing
> • Anonymization of Personal Data by the Processor\'s subprocessor, Orionis Analytics Ltd., for the purpose of generating analytics reports
> • Restriction, erasure, and destruction of Personal Data in accordance with the Controller\'s instructions and Section 12 of the DPA
**A.6 Purpose of Processing**

The purposes of the Processing are to enable the Controller to use the Processor\'s cloud hosting, managed database, and analytics services for the Controller\'s healthcare platform operations, including without limitation:
> • Hosting and operating the Controller\'s patient management systems and electronic health records
> • Providing managed database services for the Controller\'s operational and clinical databases
> • Providing disaster recovery and business continuity services to ensure the availability and resilience of the Controller\'s systems
> • Providing anonymized analytics and reporting services to support the Controller\'s operational and clinical decision-making
**A.7 Categories of Data Subjects**
The following categories of Data Subjects are affected by the Processing:

> • **Patients of the Controller:** Individuals who receive or have received healthcare services from the Controller or the Controller\'s affiliated healthcare providers, and whose Personal Data is stored in the Controller\'s patient management and electronic health records systems hosted by the Processor.

> • **Healthcare provider contacts of the Controller:** Physicians, nurses, specialists, and other healthcare professionals who interact with the Controller\'s systems, including their professional credentials, contact information, and affiliations.

> • **Employees of the Controller:** Employees of the Controller to the extent that their Personal Data is Processed in connection with the Services, including employment-related information stored in systems hosted by the Processor.
**A.8 Categories of Personal Data**
The following categories of Personal Data are Processed:
> • Full names (first name, last name, and, where applicable, middle name)
> • Dates of birth
> • Contact information, including email addresses, telephone numbers, and postal addresses
> • Health insurance identifiers and policy numbers
> • Medical record numbers and patient identification numbers
> • Diagnosis codes (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, or ICD-10)
> • Treatment histories, including records of procedures, therapies, prescriptions, and clinical notes
> • Professional credentials and affiliations of healthcare providers, including medical license numbers, National Provider Identifier (NPI) numbers, and institutional affiliations
> • Employment-related information for Controller employees, including employee identification numbers, job titles, department assignments, and work contact information
**A.9 Special Categories of Data (if applicable)**

The Processing involves special categories of Personal Data within the meaning of Article 9(1) of the GDPR. Specifically, the Processing involves data concerning health, including diagnosis codes (ICD-10), treatment histories, medical record numbers, and other clinical data that constitutes data concerning the physical or mental health of natural persons. The Controller warrants that it has established a valid legal basis for the Processing of such special categories of data in accordance with Article 9(2) of the GDPR.
**A.10 Frequency of Transfers**

Personal Data is transferred on a continuous, ongoing basis for the duration of the Agreement. Data transfers occur in real time or near-real time as part of the Processor\'s cloud hosting and managed database services.
**A.11 Retention Period**
Personal Data shall be retained and Processed by the Processor for the duration of the Agreement, subject to the deletion provisions set forth in Section 12 of the DPA.
**A.12 Subprocessors.** The following Subprocessors are authorized to Process Personal Data on behalf of the Controller as of the date of this DPA:
**Subprocessor**              **Registered Address**                                                **Location of Processing**   **Services Provided**
Larkfield Data Systems, LLC   7600 Prosperity Avenue, Fairfax, VA 22031, United States of America   Northern Virginia, USA       Database management and disaster recovery services
Orionis Analytics Ltd.        14 Fitzwilliam Square East, Dublin 2, D02 W526, Ireland               Dublin, Ireland              Anonymization and analytics services
**A.13 Technical and Organizational Measures**
The technical and organizational measures implemented by the Processor (and, as applicable, by its Subprocessors) to protect Personal Data are described in Annex B to this DPA.
**[ANNEX B --- TECHNICAL AND ORGANIZATIONAL MEASURES]{.underline}**

This Annex B forms an integral part of the Data Processing Agreement (\"DPA\") and describes the technical and organizational measures implemented by the Processor to ensure the security and protection of Personal Data Processed on behalf of the Controller. These measures are designed to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, in accordance with Article 32 of the GDPR, and are subject to ongoing review and improvement.

**B.1 Encryption. Encryption at Rest:** All Personal Data stored in the Processor\'s data centers, including data stored in databases, file systems, object storage, and backup media, is encrypted at rest using the Advanced Encryption Standard with 256-bit keys (AES-256). Encryption at rest is applied uniformly across all storage tiers and replication targets, including primary storage in Frankfurt, secondary storage in Dublin, and disaster recovery storage in Northern Virginia.

**Encryption in Transit:** All data transmissions involving Personal Data are encrypted in transit using Transport Layer Security version 1.3 (TLS 1.3) or higher. This includes transmissions between the Controller\'s systems and the Processor\'s cloud infrastructure, transmissions between the Processor\'s data centers (Frankfurt, Dublin, and Northern Virginia), and transmissions between the Processor and its Subprocessors. The Processor does not support deprecated encryption protocols (including SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1) for any connections involving Personal Data.

**Key Management:** Encryption keys are managed through a centralized key management system utilizing FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security modules (HSMs). Encryption keys are generated using cryptographically secure random number generators, stored in the HSMs, and rotated on an annual basis in accordance with the Processor\'s key rotation policy. Key access is restricted to authorized personnel on a strict need-to-know basis, with all key management operations logged and auditable.
**B.2 Access Controls**

**Role-Based Access Control (RBAC):** The Processor implements role-based access control with least-privilege principles for all systems that Process Personal Data. Access to Personal Data is granted only to those personnel whose roles require such access for the performance of the Services, and access privileges are limited to the minimum level necessary for the performance of the assigned role.

**Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):** Multi-factor authentication is required for all administrative and privileged access to systems that Process Personal Data. MFA is enforced through hardware tokens or authenticator applications; SMS-based authentication is not permitted for privileged access.

**Segregation of Duties:** Critical Processing activities, including database administration, key management, and access provisioning, are subject to segregation of duties controls. No single individual has the ability to perform all steps of a critical operation without independent verification or approval.

**Access Reviews:** The Processor\'s information security team conducts formal access reviews on a quarterly basis to verify that access privileges remain appropriate and aligned with current role assignments. Access that is no longer required is promptly revoked. Access review results are documented and retained for a minimum of three (3) years.
**B.3 Network Security**

**Firewalls and Network Segmentation:** The Processor\'s data centers employ multi-layered firewall architectures with network segmentation between client environments, management networks, and public-facing services. Each client environment is logically isolated from other client environments and from the Processor\'s internal management infrastructure.

**Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS):** The Processor deploys intrusion detection and prevention systems across all network segments. IDS/IPS systems are monitored continuously (24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year) by the Processor\'s security operations center (SOC). Alerts are triaged and escalated in accordance with the Processor\'s incident response procedures.

**Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing:** Automated vulnerability scanning is performed on a monthly basis across all systems and network segments that Process Personal Data. Critical and high-severity vulnerabilities are remediated within fourteen (14) calendar days of identification; medium-severity vulnerabilities are remediated within thirty (30) calendar days. Annual penetration testing is conducted by an independent, qualified third-party information security firm. Penetration test findings are reported to the Processor\'s Chief Information Security Officer and tracked to remediation.

**DDoS Mitigation:** The Processor employs distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) mitigation services to protect its cloud infrastructure and the Controller\'s hosted applications from volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DDoS attacks.
**B.4 Physical Security**

**Data Center Security:** All data centers utilized by the Processor (including subprocessor-operated data centers in Dublin and Northern Virginia) are equipped with the following physical security controls:
> • 24/7 on-site security personnel
> • Closed-circuit television (CCTV) surveillance with a minimum of ninety (90) days of recorded footage retention
> • Biometric access controls (fingerprint or iris scan) at all entry points to data processing areas
> • Mantrap (airlock) entry systems at primary data center entrances
> • Visitor management procedures requiring escort by authorized personnel at all times
**Environmental Controls:** Data centers are equipped with:
> • Fire detection and suppression systems (pre-action dry pipe sprinkler systems and gas-based suppression for server rooms)
> • Climate control systems maintaining optimal temperature and humidity for computing equipment
> • Redundant power supply, including uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems and on-site diesel generators with a minimum of seventy-two (72) hours of fuel reserve
> • Redundant network connectivity from multiple independent telecommunications providers
**B.5 Data Center Locations**
The Processor\'s data processing infrastructure is distributed across the following data center locations:
**Data Center**          **Location**                                  **Operator**                                 **Role**
Frankfurt, Germany       Frankfurt am Main, Hesse, Germany             Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH             Primary EU data center --- production environment, primary data storage
Dublin, Ireland          Dublin 2, Ireland                             Orionis Analytics Ltd. (Subprocessor)        Secondary EU data center --- anonymization and analytics processing
Northern Virginia, USA   Fairfax, Virginia, United States of America   Larkfield Data Systems, LLC (Subprocessor)   Disaster recovery data center --- database management, backup, and failover
**B.6 Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery**

**Geographic Redundancy:** Personal Data is replicated across geographically redundant data centers (Frankfurt, Dublin, and Northern Virginia) to ensure availability and resilience in the event of a localized outage, natural disaster, or other disruption affecting a single data center.

**Recovery Point Objective (RPO):** The Processor maintains a recovery point objective of one (1) hour, meaning that in the event of a disaster or system failure, the maximum data loss shall not exceed one (1) hour of data.

**Recovery Time Objective (RTO):** The Processor maintains a recovery time objective of four (4) hours, meaning that in the event of a disaster or system failure affecting the primary production environment, the Processor targets restoration of Services within four (4) hours.

**Disaster Recovery Testing:** The Processor conducts comprehensive disaster recovery testing at least once per year, including simulated failover to the Northern Virginia disaster recovery site. Test results are documented and reviewed by the Processor\'s Chief Information Security Officer and Chief Technology Officer.
**B.7 Personnel Security**

**Background Checks:** All Processor personnel who have access to Personal Data are subject to background checks prior to commencing employment or engagement, including verification of identity, criminal records checks (to the extent permitted by applicable law), and verification of professional qualifications where relevant.
**Confidentiality Agreements:** All Processor personnel with access to Personal Data are required to execute written confidentiality agreements in accordance with Section 4 of the DPA.

**Security Awareness Training:** All Processor personnel receive annual security awareness training covering topics including data protection principles, information security policies and procedures, social engineering and phishing awareness, incident reporting procedures, and secure data handling practices. Training completion records are maintained by the Processor\'s human resources department.
**B.8 Incident Response**

**Incident Response Plan:** The Processor maintains a documented incident response plan that is reviewed and updated at least annually. The incident response plan addresses the identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review of security incidents, including Personal Data Breaches.

**Incident Response Team:** The Processor maintains a designated incident response team that is available twenty-four (24) hours a day, seven (7) days a week, three hundred sixty-five (365) days a year. The incident response team includes representatives from information security, legal, operations, and communications functions.

**Alignment with ISO 27001:** The Processor\'s incident response procedures are aligned with the requirements of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, specifically Annex A Control A.5.24 (Information security incident management planning and preparation), A.5.25 (Assessment and decision on information security events), A.5.26 (Response to information security incidents), and A.5.27 (Learning from information security incidents).
**B.9 Certifications and Audits**

**ISO 27001:2022 Certification:** The Processor holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification, Certificate Number ISO-27001-SC-2024-0891, issued by TÜV Rheinland AG on June 15, 2024, valid through June 14, 2027. The certification covers the Processor\'s information security management system as it applies to the provision of cloud hosting, managed database, and analytics services from the Processor\'s Frankfurt data center.

**SOC 2 Type II Report:** The Processor obtains an annual SOC 2 Type II report covering the Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy). The most recent SOC 2 Type II report was dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, and was issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH. The SOC 2 Type II report is available to the Controller upon request, subject to the execution of a non-disclosure agreement where required by the Processor\'s auditor.

**Ongoing Compliance:** The Processor is committed to maintaining its ISO 27001 certification and obtaining annual SOC 2 Type II reports throughout the term of the DPA. The Processor shall promptly notify the Controller of any material findings, qualifications, or exceptions identified in any certification audit or SOC 2 examination that are relevant to the Processing of Personal Data on behalf of the Controller.
*End of Annex B --- Technical and Organizational Measures*
*--- End of Data Processing Agreement, Version 3.2 ---*
*Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH*
*January 10, 2025*
